For every moment you need translation — travel, business trips, language learning —

bring along Papago, the smart parrot that speaks many languages.

▶ The Meaning of 'Papago'

"Papago" comes from Esperanto and means "parrot," an animal known for its exceptional language abilities.

Papago currently supports translation across 14 languages: Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional), Spanish, French, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Russian, German, Italian, and Arabic.

▶ Key Features

1) Text Translation

Real-time text translation for phrases and words

2) Image Translation

Automatic recognition and translation of text in the image by taking a picture and pressing the button

3) Voice Translation

Real-time voice translation to both text and audio

4) Offline translation

Can translate even in offline

5) Conversation Translation

Simultaneously speak in each other’s language when talking one-on-one with a foreigner

6) Handwriting Translation

Handwriting translation that finds the correct word and translation when you write using your finger

7) Website Translation

Automatic translation for all content when you include the URL of a foreign website

8) Document Translation

Upload a document and get a translation that preserves the original formatting.

9) Edu

Taking a picture of the passage you want to study will create a

My Note that you can use to study passages and words

10) Papago Mini

Automatic in-screen translation by Papago Mini when you copy the text in any application

11) Dictionary

Dictionary information provided to check additional meanings other than initial translation results

Be confident anytime, anywhere with your translating partner Papago!

Papago Instagram Follow : https://www.instagram.com/papago\_naver/

· Files and Media : You can save self-taken photos on your device (only on devices with OS version 9.0 or earlier).

· Notifications: Receive notifications related to using Papago Mini, downloading word cards and offline translation content, and document translation progress. (For devices running OS version 13.0 or higher)

· Location: Check information about surrounding places from the images you take with Image Translation.

### What is the most accurate Japanese translator online?
For written Japanese text, DeepL is often considered one of the most accurate options. For casual travel phrases, Google Translate and Papago usually work well enough.

### Which app is best for spoken Japanese conversations?
VoiceTra and Maestra AI are strong options for live voice-to-voice translation, and Papago also performs well for short conversational exchanges.

DeepL is the stronger choice for European languages if you need nuanced, natural-sounding text, while iTranslate and Microsoft Translator are solid alternatives worth keeping as backups on your phone.

[By Simology Travel Desk](https://simology.io/blog/team) Updated Jul 18, 2026

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fsimology.io%2Fblog%2Ftranslation-apps-travelers-2026-google-apple-deepl-microsoft)[Share on X](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Best%20Translation%20Apps%20for%20Travel%20(2026)%3A%20Top%20Picks&url=https%3A%2F%2Fsimology.io%2Fblog%2Ftranslation-apps-travelers-2026-google-apple-deepl-microsoft)[Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fsimology.io%2Fblog%2Ftranslation-apps-travelers-2026-google-apple-deepl-microsoft)

![Translation Apps for Travelers (2025): Google, Apple, DeepL, Microsoft](https://simology.io/_blog-assets/img/simology/en/blog/translation-apps-travelers-2025-google-apple-deepl-microsoft.webp)

## Why the Right Translation App Can Make or Break Your Trip

Standing in front of a menu written entirely in Thai script, or trying to explain a medical issue to a pharmacist in rural Japan — these are the moments that remind you how powerful a good translation app really is. Language barriers are one of the most common stressors for international travelers, and the apps available in 2026 have closed that gap dramatically.

According to [Google's own data](https://blog.google/products/translate/), Google Translate now processes over 100 billion words per day across 133 languages — a staggering volume that reflects how central real-time translation has become to modern travel. Meanwhile, a 2023 survey by the [GSMA](https://www.gsma.com/) found that mobile data usage among international travelers continues to rise year over year, with translation and navigation apps ranking among the top three use cases for mobile data abroad.

**The bottom line: having the right translation app on your phone — and reliable data to run it — is as essential as packing your passport in 2026.**

Of course, many of the best features (live camera translation, voice conversation mode, real-time neural translation) require an internet connection to function at full power. That's why pairing your translation app with a travel eSIM that gives you affordable data from the moment you land is the smartest setup you can make. More on that later — first, let's dig into the apps themselves.

* * *

## What Should You Look for in a Travel Translation App?

The best travel translation app for you depends on how you travel, where you're going, and what you need to communicate. Before downloading every option on this list, consider these core criteria.

- **Language coverage**: Does it support the specific language(s) of your destination?
- **Offline capability**: Can it function without an internet connection? This matters in rural areas, on flights, and anywhere data is scarce.
- **Input methods**: Does it support text, voice, and camera (image) input? The more modes, the more flexible it is in real situations.
- **Conversation mode**: Can it handle back-and-forth spoken dialogue, not just one-way translation?
- **Accuracy**: Neural machine translation (NMT) has improved enormously, but quality still varies by language pair.
- **Price**: Most apps have free tiers; some lock premium features behind a subscription.
- **Data usage**: Some features are bandwidth-heavy. If you're on a limited data plan, offline mode is your friend.

With those criteria in mind, here are the top translation apps for travelers in 2026.

* * *

## Google Translate: Still the Best All-Rounder?

Google Translate remains the most versatile and widely used translation app in the world, and for good reason. It supports 133 languages, offers offline downloads for 70+ languages, and includes a live camera mode (called "Instant Camera") that overlays translated text directly onto your phone screen in real time — invaluable for reading menus, signs, and product labels. Voice translation and a two-person conversation mode round out a genuinely comprehensive feature set.

### Standout Features

- **Instant Camera Translation**: Point your camera at any text and see the translation overlaid live. Works offline for downloaded languages.
- **Conversation Mode**: Tap a button, speak, and the app translates to the other person's language automatically. Great for asking directions or negotiating at markets.
- **Offline Mode**: Download language packs (typically 30-80 MB each) before you travel. Offline quality is slightly lower than online, but more than sufficient for everyday situations.
- **Transcribe Mode**: Translates continuous spoken audio in real time — useful for listening to tour guides or local announcements.
- **Phrasebook**: Save useful phrases for quick access without retyping.

### Where It Falls Short

Google Translate's main weakness is nuance. For complex or formal text — legal documents, literary passages, nuanced business communication — it can produce awkward or slightly off translations, particularly for languages with complex grammar like Japanese, Hungarian, or Arabic. For everyday travel purposes, though, it's more than adequate.

**Best for**: Most travelers. Especially strong for Asian languages (Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Thai), where the camera mode is a game-changer.

* * *

## Is DeepL Worth Using for Travel?

DeepL is the gold standard for translation quality in European languages, consistently outperforming Google Translate in independent academic benchmarks for languages like German, French, Spanish, Italian, Polish, and Portuguese. If you're heading to Europe and need translations that sound natural and contextually accurate — not just technically correct — DeepL is worth adding to your toolkit.

DeepL currently supports 33 languages (as of mid-2026), which is a fraction of Google Translate's coverage. It doesn't have a camera mode or robust offline functionality in its mobile app, which limits its usefulness in many travel scenarios. But for reading emails from a hotel, translating a formal letter, or understanding a complex menu description, the quality difference is noticeable.

### DeepL Free vs. DeepL Pro

| Feature | DeepL Free | DeepL Pro |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Text translation | ✅ (limited chars) | ✅ Unlimited |
| Document translation | ✅ (3/month) | ✅ Unlimited |
| Offline mobile use | ❌ | ❌ |
| Camera/image input | ❌ | ❌ |
| Languages supported | 33 | 33 |
| Price | Free | From ~$8.74/month |

**Best for**: Travelers to Europe who need high-accuracy text translation. Pair it with Google Translate for camera and voice features. If you're planning a trip to [Western Europe](https://simology.io/esim-western-europe/), this combo is hard to beat.

* * *

## Microsoft Translator: The Best Option for Groups?

Microsoft Translator is a genuinely underrated travel app that deserves more attention. It supports 70+ languages, offers offline packs, and includes a standout feature called **multi-person conversation mode** — up to 100 people can join a shared translation session using their own devices, with each person speaking in their own language and seeing translations on their screen. For group travel, guided tours, or business meetings, this is uniquely powerful.

The app's translation quality is solid (powered by the same Azure AI engine used in Microsoft's enterprise products) and its interface is clean and intuitive. It also integrates with Microsoft Office apps, which is useful for business travelers who need to translate documents on the go.

### Key Features

- **Multi-person conversation**: Share a code, everyone joins, real-time multilingual conversation.
- **Offline packs**: Available for 40+ languages.
- **Phrasebook**: Built-in common phrases organized by category (greetings, directions, food, emergencies).
- **Text-to-speech**: Hear the correct pronunciation of translated phrases.
- **Apple Watch support**: Translate directly from your wrist.

**Best for**: Group travelers, business travelers, and anyone who wants a solid Google Translate alternative with a cleaner interface.

* * *

## iTranslate: Is It Worth Paying For?

iTranslate has been around since 2009 and has built a loyal following among travelers who prefer a polished, dedicated translation experience. The free version covers basic text translation across 100+ languages, but the real value is in **iTranslate Pro** (~$5.99/month or ~$39.99/year), which unlocks offline mode, voice-to-voice translation, verb conjugation tables, and a romanization feature that shows you how to pronounce words phonetically.

The romanization feature is particularly useful in countries with non-Latin scripts — Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Greece, Russia — where even knowing how to _say_ a word can help you communicate with locals who don't read English.

iTranslate also offers **iTranslate Converse**, a separate app designed specifically for real-time spoken conversation translation, similar to a digital interpreter. It's optimized for low-latency voice translation and works well in noisy environments like markets and restaurants.

**Best for**: Travelers willing to pay for a premium experience, particularly those visiting countries with non-Latin scripts. A good pick if you're heading to [Japan](https://simology.io/esim-japan/) or [South Korea](https://simology.io/esim-south-korea/).

* * *

## Papago: The Best App for East Asian Languages?

If you're traveling to South Korea, Japan, or China, Papago (developed by Naver, South Korea's dominant search engine) is worth downloading alongside Google Translate. Papago is widely regarded as the most accurate translator for Korean, Japanese, Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, and Indonesian — languages where the linguistic distance from English is large and nuance matters enormously.

Papago supports 15 languages total, which limits its usefulness outside Asia, but within that region it consistently outperforms Google Translate on colloquial phrases, informal speech, and culturally specific expressions. Its image translation and conversation modes are also excellent.

**Best for**: Travelers to East and Southeast Asia. Free, with no meaningful paywalled features.

* * *

## Speak & Translate / Offline Translator: Niche but Useful

A handful of smaller apps round out the landscape for specific use cases:

- **Speak & Translate** (iOS): Excellent voice translation with a clean interface. Strong for quick spoken exchanges. Requires a subscription for full access.

## Do Translation Apps Work Without Internet?

Most translation apps can function offline, but with important limitations. Offline mode requires you to download language packs in advance (usually over Wi-Fi), and the quality of offline translation is generally lower than online — particularly for voice and camera features that rely on cloud-based neural models.

Here's the practical breakdown:

- **Google Translate offline**: Download language packs before you travel. Text and camera translation work offline; voice conversation mode requires a connection for best results.
- **Microsoft Translator offline**: Similar to Google — download packs in advance. Text translation works well offline.

- **Waygo**: Fully offline for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean character recognition — a unique advantage.

The right app often depends on where you're going. Here's a quick destination-by-destination guide.

### Japan

Japan is one of the most challenging destinations for English speakers, with three writing systems (hiragana, katakana, kanji) and limited English signage outside major cities. **Google Translate's camera mode** is indispensable here — it can read restaurant menus, train signs, and product labels in real time. **Papago** and **iTranslate** are strong secondary options. **Google Translate** and **Papago** are the top choices here. Thai and Vietnamese scripts are particularly well-handled by Google's camera mode. Download offline packs for Thai and Vietnamese before you go — connectivity in rural areas can be patchy.

### Middle East (Arabic)

Arabic is notoriously difficult to translate accurately due to its many dialects. **Google Translate** handles Modern Standard Arabic reasonably well but struggles with regional dialects (Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf). **Microsoft Translator** is a solid alternative. For travelers heading to the [Middle East and North Africa](https://simology.io/esim-middle-east-and-north-africa/), downloading offline Arabic packs is strongly recommended.

Both **Google Translate** and **DeepL** handle Spanish and Portuguese excellently. The main consideration is regional dialect variation — Mexican Spanish differs from Argentine Spanish, and Brazilian Portuguese differs from European Portuguese. Google Translate generally handles these regional variants better than DeepL.

## How Much Data Do Translation Apps Actually Use?

This is a practical question that matters if you're on a limited data plan. Here's a rough guide to data consumption by feature:

- **Text translation (online)**: Negligible — less than 1 KB per query.
- **Voice translation**: ~50-200 KB per exchange, depending on audio length.
- **Camera/live translation**: ~1-5 MB per minute of active use.
- **Downloading offline language packs**: 30-100 MB per language (one-time, best done over Wi-Fi).

**1\. Download offline packs before you leave home.**
Don't wait until you're at the airport or already abroad. Download language packs over Wi-Fi at home. For a trip to Japan, download Japanese. For a multi-country Europe trip, download French, German, Italian, and Spanish.

**2\. Use camera mode for menus and signs, voice mode for conversations.**
Camera translation is faster and less intrusive than typing. Voice conversation mode is better for back-and-forth exchanges with locals. Match the input method to the situation.

**3\. Speak slowly and clearly for voice translation.**
Translation apps perform significantly better when you speak at a moderate pace with clear enunciation. Avoid slang, idioms, and contractions when possible.

**4\. Cross-check important translations.**
If you're translating something important — a medical instruction, a legal document, a contract — cross-check it with a second app. No single app is infallible.

**5\. Learn 10-15 key phrases in the local language.**
Apps are tools, not replacements for basic cultural effort. Knowing how to say "please," "thank you," "how much?", "where is the bathroom?", and "I don't understand" in the local language goes a long way with locals and makes your app usage feel less robotic.

**6\. Keep your phone charged.**
Camera translation and voice features are battery-intensive. Carry a power bank, especially on long sightseeing days.

**7\. Use a travel eSIM for uninterrupted connectivity.**
The best translation features require data. A travel eSIM gives you affordable, reliable local data without the need to hunt for SIM cards or pay carrier roaming rates. You can activate it before you leave home and be online the moment your plane lands.

Camera translation is one of Papago's most-used features:

**Real-time Overlay.** Point camera at text, see translation overlaid in real-time. Works for signs, menus, labels, documents.

**Static Image Translation.** Take or upload a photo, get it translated.

**Document Scanning.** Scan multi-page documents for translation.

**Handwriting Recognition.** Some support for handwritten text (limited accuracy).

**Low Light.** Works reasonably in low light conditions.

**Tourist Essential.** For travelers in Korea, Japan, or China who don't read the language, camera translation is transformative — understand menus, navigate signs, read labels.

The implementation is smooth and the translation quality from images is good. This feature alone makes Papago essential for Asian travel.

## Voice translation

Papago's voice capabilities:

**Voice-to-Text Translation.** Speak in one language, get translated text.

**Text-to-Voice.** Hear translations spoken with natural pronunciation.

**Conversation Mode.** Two-way voice translation for face-to-face conversation between speakers of different languages.

**Noise Handling.** Reasonable performance in moderately noisy environments.

**Accent Handling.** Works with various accents within supported languages.

**Voice Options.** Male and female voice options for different languages.

For travel situations — asking directions, ordering food, basic conversation — voice translation works practically well.

## Offline capability

Papago supports offline translation:

**Language Packs.** Download packs for major language pairs (Korean-English, Japanese-English, Chinese-English, etc.).

**Pack Size.** Several hundred MB per pair, manageable on modern phones.

**Quality.** Slightly less accurate than online translation but functional for most needs.

**Travel Value.** Essential for traveling in countries without reliable international data.

**Selective Download.** Choose only the pairs you need.

For travelers, offline mode is a core reason to use Papago — airports, subways, rural areas where data is unavailable.

## Naver ecosystem context

Papago is part of Naver's broader internet ecosystem:

**Naver.** Korea's dominant search engine and portal (Korean equivalent of Google).

**LINE.** Japanese messaging app, related through Naver/SoftBank joint venture history.

**Webtoon.** Naver's comics platform, global leader in webcomics.

**HyperCLOVA.** Naver's large language model, increasingly integrated with Naver products.

**Naver Cloud.** Enterprise platform where Papago is available via API.

**Naver Dictionary.** Integrated with Papago for word-level lookups.

For Korean users and users of Naver services, Papago integrates naturally. For users outside Naver's ecosystem, Papago works as a standalone translation app.

## How Papago compares

**Against Google Translate:** Google has more languages (100+) and more integrations. Papago is better for Korean, Japanese, Chinese. For maximum coverage, Google. For Asian language depth, Papago.

**Against DeepL:** DeepL is best for European languages — German, French, Spanish, Italian. Papago is best for Asian languages. Different specializations. Both excellent in their domains.

**Against Microsoft Translator:** Microsoft has strong Office integration and business features. Papago is more consumer/travel focused. Different use cases.

**Against Apple Translate:** Apple's built-in iOS feature has improved but covers fewer languages and lacks some features. Convenient for iOS users; Papago is still better for Asian languages.

**Against \[ChatGPT\](/openai) (and other AI chatbots):** AI chatbots can translate but aren't specialized for it. Papago specializes in translation. For nuanced translation work, Papago often better; for creative language work or contextual translation, AI chatbots flexible.

## Who should use Papago

**Korean language learners and users** — top choice.

**Japanese and Chinese language work** — excellent.

**Asian travelers** (Korea, Japan, China, Taiwan) — essential.

**Korean business communication** — best quality.

**K-pop, K-drama, and Korean content consumers** — understand content accurately.

**Researchers of Asian culture** — translate documents and sources.

## Who should skip Papago

**European language users** — DeepL or Google Translate better.

**Maximum coverage needs** — Google Translate for obscure languages.

**Business enterprise users** — Microsoft Translator for Office integration.

**Users wanting AI chat** — Papago is translation-focused, not conversational AI.

## The verdict

Papago is the best mobile translation app for Korean, Japanese, and Chinese — clear and strong recommendation. For anyone who frequently translates between English and these Asian languages, or who travels in East Asia, Papago is essential.

The limitations are about scope, not quality. Papago doesn't try to be everything. It covers about 15 major languages with depth rather than 100+ languages with variable quality. For European languages, DeepL or Google Translate may serve better. For maximum language coverage, Google Translate has no rival.

The free pricing makes Papago accessible to everyone, and the lack of ads keeps the experience clean. Naver's monetization through their broader ecosystem means Papago doesn't need to aggressively monetize users.

In the translation app landscape, Papago occupies a specific but important position: the specialist's specialist for East Asian languages. For users who need what it does, nothing beats it. For users with different language needs, alternatives serve better.

In the broader AI landscape, Papago is an example of how specialized AI applications can succeed against broader competitors. Google Translate has resources Papago can't match, but Papago's focus on Asian languages lets it outperform in its specialty. This pattern — focused products beating general products in specific domains — is common in consumer AI and likely to continue.

For practical usage: if you work with Korean, Japanese, or Chinese, install Papago. If you don't, you might still use it occasionally for travel. For everything else, other tools.

## Frequently asked questions

What is Papago?+

Papago is a mobile translation app developed by Naver, South Korea's largest internet company. Launched in 2017, it has become the most-used translation app in Korea and a major competitor to Google Translate across Asia. Free to use with strong Asian language capabilities.

Is Papago better than Google Translate?+

For Korean, Japanese, and Chinese translations, Papago is generally better than Google Translate — more natural, culturally appropriate, and accurate. For European languages, Google Translate is often better. For maximum language coverage, Google Translate has more languages.

Is Papago free?+

Yes — completely free with no subscriptions required. No ads in the mobile apps. Naver monetizes through its broader ecosystem, not Papago subscriptions.

What languages does Papago support?+

Around 15 major languages — Korean, English, Japanese, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Spanish, French, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Russian, Italian, German, Portuguese, Hindi. Fewer than Google Translate but deeper quality in supported languages.

Can Papago translate images?+

Yes — camera-based translation works excellently. Point your camera at a menu, sign, or document and Papago translates in real-time overlay. Especially useful for travelers in Korea, Japan, China where English signage is limited.

Does Papago work offline?+

Yes — you can download offline packs for core language pairs (Korean-English, Japanese-English, Chinese-English). Offline translation is slightly less accurate than online but works without data connection. Useful for travel.

How does Papago compare to DeepL?+

DeepL is best for European languages (German, French, Spanish). Papago is best for Asian languages (Korean, Japanese, Chinese). For Korean work specifically, Papago is typically better than DeepL. Different tools for different language needs.

Why is it called Papago?+

The Google Translate translation

Technology is a relatively new, multifaceted term, the exact definition of which escapes due to the constant development of the meaning of this concept, both in itself and taken in relations with others, the same broad concepts: culture, society, politics, religion, nature [4 ]. By the early twentieth century, the term "technology" encompassed a collection of tools, processes, and ideas in addition to tools and machines. By the middle of the century, the concept was defined by phrases such as "the means or activity by which a person changes his environment and manipulates it" [5].

My evaluation

In my opinion, the current DeepL version of the Russian has an edge over the Google Translate version, although both had a problem translating the term “совокупность средств,” rendering it as “set of tools” (DeepL) and “collection of tools” (GT). Although “средства” can properly be translated as “tools” in some contexts, the sentence also contains the word “инструменты,” which unambiguously conveys the sense of “tools.” A human would not use “tools” twice in the same sentence as both MT systems have done. To be fair, however, “средства” has such a wide range of meanings that it can present difficulties for a human translator as well. In this context, a more general English term would probably be better. I would probably use “equipment.” Incidentally, both DeepL and GT translated “средства” properly as “means” in the last sentence.

One final point: Google Translate functions quite well as an online multilingual dictionary when individual words are entered. DeepL does not. Linguee, which owns DeepL, does, however, include a very useful dictionary function.

Съвременните технологии са свързани с [науката](https://bg.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9D%D0%B0%D1%83%D0%BA%D0%B0) и могат да бъдат обособени като отделна [академична дисциплина](https://bg.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%90%D0%BA%D0%B0%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BC%D0%B8%D1%87%D0%BD%D0%B0_%D0%B4%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%86%D0%B8%D0%BF%D0%BB%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%B0), насочена към разработване и усъвършенстване на методите и инструментите за производство. Technology is a relatively new, multifaceted term, the exact definition of which eludes us because of the constant evolution of the meaning of this concept, both in itself and taken in relationship to other, equally broad concepts: culture, society, politics, religion, nature\[4\]. By the beginning of the twentieth century, the term "technology" encompassed a set of tools, processes, and ideas in addition to tools and machines. By mid-century the concept was defined in such phrases as "the means or activities by which man alters and manipulates his environment."\[5\]

The Google Translate translation

Technology is a relatively new, multifaceted term, the exact definition of which escapes due to the constant development of the meaning of this concept, both in itself and taken in relations with others, the same broad concepts: culture, society, politics, religion, nature \[4 \]. By the early twentieth century, the term "technology" encompassed a collection of tools, processes, and ideas in addition to tools and machines. By the middle of the century, the concept was defined by phrases such as "the means or activity by which a person changes his environment and manipulates it" \[5\].

My evaluation

In my opinion, the current DeepL version of the Russian has an edge over the Google Translate version, although both had a problem translating the term “совокупность средств,” rendering it as “set of tools” (DeepL) and “collection of tools” (GT). Although “средства” can properly be translated as “tools” in some contexts, the sentence also contains the word “инструменты,” which unambiguously conveys the sense of “tools.” A human would not use “tools” twice in the same sentence as both MT systems have done. To be fair, however, “средства” has such a wide range of meanings that it can present difficulties for a human translator as well. In this context, a more general English term would probably be better. I would probably use “equipment.” Incidentally, both DeepL and GT translated “средства” properly as “means” in the last sentence.

One final point: Google Translate functions quite well as an online multilingual dictionary when individual words are entered. DeepL does not. Linguee, which owns DeepL, does, however, include a very useful dictionary function.

## Test-Driving Japanese Translation Apps for Japan Travel
### Image Translation
To its credit, PapaGo performs much better than Google Translate when it comes to deciphering handwritten text, even if what comes out is barely understandable or outright inaccurate.

### Voice Translation
Google Translate’s voice recognition is surprisingly good. It picks up English sentences accurately as long as you speak quite clearly, and the resulting translations are fine.

Though it ultimately doesn’t make too much difference, PapaGo’s Japanese (female) voice rings clear and cheerful.

In this case, PapaGo’s rendering was the most natural, using Japanese that the average speaker would most likely use.

The first three sentences from PapaGo above resulted from attempts to ask for directions to the ryokan – “real kind” was possibly the closest it came.

This was also true of Google Translate’s voice recognition, though it outperforms PapaGo in these terms if you’re willing to try a few times.

## Final thoughts
If you wanted to choose just one app for traveling in Japan, PapaGo would be a decent contender.

If you’d rather speak into the phone than type your text in, Google Translate probably has the edge on the other apps, but only by a slight margin. PapaGo and Japanese Translation also perform well when it comes to voice translation.

For better-than-average translations, Japanese Translation is a good choice, especially for anyone who’s actually learning Japanese.

## Japanese–English and English–Japanese Translation Apps for iPhones

There are quite literally hundreds of translation apps out there. The goal was to find useful, intuitive apps that non-Japanese speakers could use to communicate with locals, figure out what’s what, and generally get around. For this reason, I didn’t include grammar-focused Japanese-learning apps, ‘phrasebook’ apps, or dictionary apps.

I took six translation apps out into the Tokyo wilderness for a spin. These were downloaded from the App Store on an iPhone, though some of these will also be available on Android. I’ve noted wherever this is the case.

In no particular order, these are the apps I tested:

### 1\. Google Translate

There are three main parts to this app: photo, voice, and text translation. Using this app, you point your phone camera at the text you want to read, and the optical character recognition (OCR) technology “reads” the text and displays the translation directly on your phone screen, displacing the original text. You can also type in English text that will be translated into Japanese (or other languages) and vice versa.

There’s also an option to speak into the phone’s inbuilt microphone. Google Translate records and renders your words into text, then produces a translation. This is then read out to you in the target language. Google Translate also works offline. It’s available on [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/google-translate/id414706506) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.google.android.apps.translate&hl=en) (but of course) and is free for use.

### 2\. Waygo

This app allows you to write or ‘draw’ kanji characters onto the screen. This does rely on some prior knowledge of Japanese, Chinese, or Korean characters. You are also able to hold the phone up to a given text or set of words and have Waygo render a translation. The app limits you to 10 free translations a day; beyond this, you’ll need to purchase the app. Available on [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/waygo-chinese-japanese-and-korean-translator/id496038103). There’s also an [official website](http://www.waygoapp.com/).

### 3\. iTranslate

This app offers text, voice, and photo translation. While you can translate between English and Japanese, there are around 40 language pairs available. As a bonus, it works offline once you’ve downloaded the requisite language packs. I tested this with a free trial of the paid version. Available on [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/itranslate-translator/id288113403) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=at.nk.tools.iTranslate&hl=en).

### 4\. PapaGo

Developed by Naver, this app does text, voice, and photo translation. It also allows you to have a simultaneous conversation in two languages using the app. You’ll be passing the phone back and forth between you and another person speaking a different language into the phone. PapaGo also translates between various Asian languages, including Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, and Chinese. If you’re traveling around Asia, you might want to check this out. You will need to be connected to the internet to use this app, but on the bright side, it’s free. Available on [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/naver-papago-ai-translator/id1147874819) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.naver.labs.translator&hl=en).

### 5\. Japanese Translator Offline

In this app, you’ll type in the sentence you need and it spits out a Japanese rendering for you. You can also speak into the app. As the name suggests, you won’t need WiFi to use this. It’s a free app. At this point in time, to our knowledge, this is [iOS only](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/japanese-translator-offline/id998183091).

### 6\. Photo Translator + +

This is the companion app to Japanese Translation, also by Evolly.app. You can either upload a photo with Japanese text from your camera library or take a photo of what you’re looking at, and it will give you a translation superimposed on top of the original text. This particular free app will require you to watch the occasional video ad (30 seconds at most, and usually about 10 seconds), but it’s a small price to pay. Available on [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/photo-translator/id1350347947) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=xbean.image.picture.translate.ocr&hl=en_US).

## What makes a useful Japanese translation travel app?

The real test, of course, is:

- a) how practical they are when you’re actually traveling around Japan
- b) how useful they are for communicating
- c) how easy and intuitive the apps themselves are to use. I’ve compared these apps by their respective functions.

These are a few of the criteria I considered when testing the apps:

### Text translation:

- If I typed in English sentences, would they be translated into accurate or understandable Japanese?
- Similarly, if a native Japanese speaker typed in something, would the English rendering be accurate?

### Image translation:

- How good is the app at deciphering and capturing Japanese text?
- Would the app be able to render this text into understandable English?
- Could the app read handwritten menus and signs?

### Voice translation:

- How accurately can the app decipher English-language sentences spoken into the phone?
- How accurate were the Japanese translations of our words?
- Would this be as accurate for Japanese speakers?

## Test-Driving Japanese Translation Apps for Japan Travel

![Examples of English to Japanese translations using Google Translate](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-hfgd79p/0/2243fb6e/L/i-hfgd79p-L.jpg)

Using Google Translate’s text input © Florentyna Leow

### Text Translation

Google Translate has improved in leaps and bounds over the last few years, which is evident in the above-average quality of its translations. It does reasonably well with sentences a traveler might potentially ask. For the best results – and this is true of all the apps below – you want to communicate in simple sentences that leave no room for ambiguity.

In the same way, Japanese to English translations work best with uncomplicated sentences and concepts. You might not be having deep, philosophical conversations with another local – unless you’re willing to sit down for a good length of time – but you will at least find out where the nearest bathroom is.

![Examples of English to Japanese translations using iTranslate Pro’s text input](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-hdr38mQ/0/66f63a3b/L/i-hdr38mQ-L.jpg)

Using iTranslate Pro’s text input © Florentyna Leow

iTranslate fared decently, though the translations that emerge aren’t always 100% correct. For instance, in the middle example, the word for “top up” is translated to “上げる” or “raise,” which doesn’t make any sense in Japanese. Contextually, someone might eventually understand it. If you receive a puzzled look in return when you show them a translated sentence, your intended meaning might have been lost in translation, so consider rephrasing.

Something else I noticed with iTranslate is that it does not always perform well with compound sentences. The third sentence above has two parts: defining ‘warabimochi’ and asking if it’s vegan. The translation that emerged only translated the first half of the sentence and not the second. This is something that can happen with translation apps generally, so you’ll want to keep your queries and statements short and simple.

![Examples of English to Japanese translations using Japanese Translator Offline](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-3JSbn9W/0/3073e260/L/i-3JSbn9W-L.jpg)

Using Japanese Translator Offline © Florentyna Leow

As expected of an app specializing in Japanese–English translations, this performed well. The interface is clean and straightforward. The Japanese translations the app gives you are generally on the formal side, but that’s an observation rather than a complaint. It’s great for casual travelers. But, this is also a useful app for beginner to intermediate learners of Japanese, as you’ll see not only what you wanted translated, but also similar example sentences to reinforce your learning.

Additionally, it’s worth mentioning that Japanese Translator Offline is good at capturing sentences spoken into the app – I tested all the examples above by typing and speaking them in. It works well with Japanese-language input too.

![Examples of English to Japanese translations using PapaGo](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-RJvgWQs/0/f48ef4c8/L/i-RJvgWQs-L.jpg)

Text translations for PapaGo © Florentyna Leow

Not only were they accurate, PapaGos’s Japanese translations of our text-based queries were some of the most natural-sounding out of all the apps we used. They won’t always be ‘formal’ but they sound like someone you might actually hear talking on the street, which is a nice bonus. The app itself is also easy to use, with colour-coded and easily understandable functions.

### Image Translation

![Japanese to English translation of a Dyson vacuum cleaner box using Google Translate’s image function](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-93VN9BG/0/cfb654f3/L/i-93VN9BG-L.jpg)

Reading text on a Dyson vacuum cleaner box with Google Translate © Florentyna Leow

I had high hopes for Google Translate’s much-feted Word Lens. I trained the phone camera on printed text on the side of a Dyson vacuum cleaner box to reasonably clear results. The translation wasn’t perfect – the first sentence is more accurately rendered as “Continuing to challenge  even with repeated failures” – but the technology itself is impressive.

![Four examples of Japanese to English image translations using Google Translate](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-fRkh3wH/0/557da17e/L/i-fRkh3wH-L.jpg)

Four instances of using Google Translate in the wild © Florentyna Leow

Word Lens produces decent on-the-spot translations when you hover over clear, printed text. But you have mixed results in various real-life situations. The menu on the left is imperfectly translated, and the non-Japanese reader would be hard-pressed to order from it, though the app did its best with the vertical text.

The third example above (second to right) shows Word Lens trying to interpret a handwritten menu. In general, the app does not do well (yet) hovering over handwritten text regardless of legibility, so it’s not useful in many Japanese restaurants. It does better when you take a photo of something and use the app to read it from your library.

Still, if you just want to figure out what flavour of chocolate you’re buying from the convenience store (far right), Google Translate’s photo function doesn’t do too badly.

![Three examples of Japanese to English image translations using Waygo](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-7GkDqmm/0/373eae56/L/i-7GkDqmm-L.jpg)

Using Waygo in the wild © Florentyna Leow

For all the praise it has received for its East Asia-specific character recognition, Waygo was surprisingly unhelpful when it came to practical use in Japan. It was able to read some printed text but not most things I trained the camera on, whether handwritten, printed, vertical, or horizontal.

![Four different examples of Japanese to English image translations using Waygo](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-d393J7K/0/3463cf75/L/i-d393J7K-L.jpg)

More instances of using Waygo. From left to right: a sandwich board, a handwritten menu, a train ticket, and an entrance ticket to the Golden Pavilion © Florentyna Leow

In more cases than not, it was unable to detect any text or find any translations for the text I looked at. There was just one occasion where it managed to translate something accurately! The OCR technology just was not up to par with some of the other apps I tried out.

Waygo is purportedly useful for language learners in East Asia when it comes to identifying kanji characters, especially in China. But if you’re looking for a straightforward and intuitive translation app for Japan travel, Waygo isn’t it – especially not with just 10 free translations a day. Given the existence of other better apps out there, you can skip this.

With PapaGo’s photo translation function, you point your phone camera at a scene or text that you want to read. Once you snap a photo, the app scans it for any text and highlights any Japanese text in white outlined box. You can then tap on each highlighted box to read what it says.

To its credit, PapaGo performs much better than Google Translate when it comes to deciphering handwritten text, even if what comes out is barely understandable or outright inaccurate. The middle translation is just on the mark; the second should read “please cooperate and queue.”

![Three more examples of Japanese to English image translations using the PapaGo app](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-nxSC9Qc/0/92aacbdb/L/i-nxSC9Qc-L.jpg)

More instances of using PapaGo in the wild © Florentyna Leow

The left translation should have read “mutton keema” towards the end, and 温玉 is an onsen egg rather than a “hot ball” – but it’s possible to at least get an idea of what’s on the menu, even if it’s written on a chalkboard in vertical text.

Also, ‘salmon-bashing warship’ is a direct translation of what’s written there, even if it actually refers to gunkan-style sushi with chopped salmon.

![Four examples of Japanese to English image translations using iTranslate](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-2MWXsJp/0/6081e692/L/i-2MWXsJp-L.jpg)

iTranslate’s results are a mixed bag when it comes to image translations © Florentyna Leow

Out of all the apps here, iTranslate proved the least useful for image translations. Sometimes it wouldn’t be able to detect any printed text in the image, and when it did, it wasn’t the most pleasant to read. If you tried to move the borders of the white box on the screen, your translation would disappear. It’s not the most intuitive app around.

What is so far true across all the apps I tested, though, is that they’re not great at picking up Japanese words mixed in with English sentences. ‘Ryokan,’ which refers to a Japanese-style inn, proved to be a good test for the voice recognition function – it’s not easy for non-Japanese speakers to pronounce accurately.

The first three sentences from PapaGo above resulted from attempts to ask for directions to the ryokan – “real kind” was possibly the closest it came. Saying it in Japanese, on the other hand, produced perfectly understandable results.

Asking for directions to the inn © Florentyna Leow

This was also true of Google Translate’s voice recognition, though it outperforms PapaGo in these terms if you’re willing to try a few times. It took several attempts for it to understand that I was saying ‘ryokan’ instead of ‘dokkan,’ ‘Yukon,’ ‘know you can,’ and other variants.

![Testing out Japanese words mixed into English sentences with the PapaGo translation app](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-h8TzrsW/0/59a338d9/L/i-h8TzrsW-L.jpg)

Testing out Japanese words mixed into English sentences © Florentyna Leow

I also asked a friend to say some sentences with Japanese words mixed in to the English. To wit, the original sentences spoken into PapaGo above were:

- 1) I need a bowl of sukiyaki (beef and vegetables cooked in soy, sugar, and sake)
- 2) Where is the kissaten (a retro Japanese-style cafe)
- 3) I would like the tempura please.

![Side-by-side comparison of asking for directions to Meiji-jingumae Station, using the iTranslate Pro, PapaGo, and Google Translate phone translation apps](https://photos.smugmug.com/photos/i-24zPhrm/0/f993d798/L/i-24zPhrm-L.jpg)

Asking for directions to Meiji-jingumae Station © Florentyna Leow

When it came to asking for directions to Meiji-jingumae Station, only Google Translate managed to pick up something approximate. The rest of the apps didn’t quite pan out. (One of the attempts with Japanese Translator Offline came out with the chuckle-inducing “which way to make you think of my station.”)

Why should this be the case? The short answer is that the technology for machines to recognize several languages in a single sentence just hasn’t reached the point where it can displace multilingual humans. (On the bright side, it means that interpreters won’t be out of a job just yet.)

What this means for an app user: for best results, speak clearly, in simple English-only sentences with key words that communicate exactly what you’re trying to say. If you have place names or particular words in Japanese you want to say, a typed translation is likely to give you better results than a spoken one.

## Final thoughts

Is there a particular app I would recommend? For people with an iPhone who just want to be able to translate text (menus etc), the built-in iPhone translation app is probably all you need. As for the other apps discussed here, each had their strengths and weaknesses. None of them were 100% accurate – they all had their fair share of funny errors and misunderstandings. But, outside of Waygo, most of the apps on this list performed quite well. Most of them were available for offline use, but they worked best when the phone was connected to WiFi. Choosing one will boil down to personal preference: whether you like the interface, what you’re using it for, and whether it gets the job done for you.

If you wanted to choose just one app for traveling in Japan, PapaGo would be a decent contender. It’s the most natural-sounding out of all the apps above – and the voice issuing from the app actually sounds quite friendly – so it’s useful for communicating with locals. It also fared reasonably well in practical situations like reading menus and deciphering signs. The only real downside is that you’d need to have pocket WiFi to use this app on the ground.

If you’d rather speak into the phone than type your text in, Google Translate probably has the edge on the other apps, but only by a slight margin. PapaGo and Japanese Translation also perform well when it comes to voice translation.

For better-than-average translations, Japanese Translation is a good choice, especially for anyone who’s actually learning Japanese. As I’ve shown above, the app gives you not just a translation but also related examples existing in its database. The accompanying Photo Translator app by the same company (Evolly) is great for image translations, especially if you want to understand entire paragraphs in a single go – for example, to read printed signboards for an artifact or attraction.

Bear in mind that these translation apps are technologies in flux. A few years ago, machine translation wasn’t capable of producing translations that made any sense; they’ve now reached the point where they’ve begun to be more useful out in the field. I expect that all of the apps above will continue to improve with time.

So, download a couple of them for your travels in Japan and have fun with them. The most important thing with these translation apps to actually use them in the wild. Any of these will make communicating with people that much easier, and as a bonus, you might end up with a few hilarious gaffes and stories at the end of it.

Japan’s language barrier can feel incredibly intimidating.

Whether you’re looking at a restaurant menu that’s only in kanji, staring blankly at a train station sign, or trying to use a vending machine, the struggle is real… as is the need for a translation app.

But what I’ve discovered after a dozen trips to Japan is that one translation app isn’t enough.

Nowadays, when I visit Japan, I use a combination of three apps. Together, help me order meals, navigate train stations, read signs, and have simple conversations with locals.

Here’s exactly which three I use, and what each one does better than the rest.

In this article

[Toggle](https://esim.holafly.com/travel-tips/translation-apps-japan-travel/#)

## Why one translation app is never enough in Japan

![A man holds a smartphone displaying a language translation interface with multilingual chat bubbles floating above the screen.](https://media.holafly.com/sites/1/2026/07/smartphone-translation-app-japan-travel.jpg)Translation apps each have different strengths — the trick to getting around Japan smoothly is knowing which one to open for reading, writing, or speaking.

One of the biggest mistakes I made on my [first trip to Japan](https://esim.holafly.com/travel-tips/how-to-plan-first-trip-japan/) was assuming a single translation app could handle everything. When that app didn’t work in a way I needed it to, I’d download another one, then another.

What I realized through trying dozens of translation and [travel apps in Japan](https://esim.holafly.com/travel-tips/apps-travel-japan/) is that they all have different strengths.

Some are excellent at instantly translating signs through your camera, but struggle with longer passages of text. Others help you speak to locals in real-time, but aren’t much help when you’re trying to work out what a vending machine or train ticket machine says.

So the key to efficient translation in Japan is knowing which app helps with what.

There are **3 core language barrier issues** in Japan: **reading, writing, and talking**. I now use a different app for each issue, and together they cover almost every language challenge I’ve encountered in Japan.

## Google Translate, the one I pull out in front of every menu and vending machine

Google Translate is the translation app I use the most in daily life when I’m in Japan. It’s the one I instinctively reach for whenever I’m faced with an all-kanji [Tokyo street food](https://esim.holafly.com/travel-tips/tokyo-street-food/) vendor, a vending machine full of unfamiliar drinks, or a train ticket machine that doesn’t have an English language option.

The **live camera translation feature** makes translating quick and easy. You simply point your camera and get an instant translation.

That being said, for long sentences or paragraphs, the live camera mode can take several seconds to find the most accurate translation. And even then, it doesn’t always give the most natural or easy-to-understand sentence.

This problem is especially apparent in dimly lit restaurants. Without enough light, it struggles to recognize the text accurately.

Therefore, for more accurate translations, it is often better to **take a photo first, then use Google Translate to scan the image**.

Aside from the camera feature, **voice translation** is super helpful when speaking with a taxi driver, asking for directions, or having any other short interactions with locals.

Another advantage of Google Translate is that you can **download the Japanese language pack** before you travel. This allows you to use the app when you’re without data or signal. That being said, some features become noticeably less reliable offline, so you’ll get the best results when you have an internet connection.

## DeepL, the one I trust for anything longer than a sentence

While Google Translate is my go-to for menus, road signs, and other quick translations on the move, DeepL is the translation app I use to **translate longer pieces of Japanese.**

Because translating Japanese to English requires transliteration (translating between writing systems/alphabets), many translation apps produce clunky or confusing translations.

DeepL, however, does a superb job of **translating full sentences and paragraphs in a way that flows naturally.** So I use this app for more complex travel needs like:

- Messaging an accommodation host
- Understanding a printed notice or hotel information sheet
- Writing a polite request

Aside from real-time camera and photo translations, you can translate via voice or text. The text translation also gives you **alternative ways to say things**, such as if you want to sound more formal or polite.

The downside of DeepL, however, is that there is no offline mode; the app requires an internet connection for all translation features.

## Papago, my quiet favorite for actually talking to people

Papago is one of the least-known translation apps, but when it comes to transliterating languages like Japanese, it’s one of the most reliable apps out there.

Developed by the South Korean company Naver, **Papago was built with Asian languages in mind.** As a result, it handles conversational Japanese much more naturally than other apps.

Papago’s **conversation mode** is its best feature, helping you have short interactions with locals in a smooth, natural way without sounding awkward or robotic. You simply pass the phone back and forth, so both people can speak in their own language and see the translation almost instantly.

Hence, this is the app I reach for when I need **any type of verbal translation,** such as:

- Asking for directions
- Chatting with shop staff
- Checking into a hotel or guesthouse
- Asking simple questions in cafés and restaurants

That said, I wouldn’t rely on Papago for everything. Google Translate remains much faster for reading menus and signs through your camera, while DeepL is my first choice for translating longer pieces of text or writing messages that need to sound natural.

## How I set up all three before I fly

![A traveler seated at a restaurant table holds a menu in one hand and a phone running a translation app in the other.](https://media.holafly.com/sites/1/2026/07/tourist-using-translation-app-restaurant-menu-japan.jpg)Testing your apps before you land — ideally in airplane mode — means you’ll know exactly what works offline when you’re facing an all-kanji menu.

After a dozen trips, I’ve settled on this specific three-way system that covers every travel situation I encounter in Japan:

- **Google Translate** to **read** menus, signs, and other everyday short texts.
- **DeepL** to **write** messages and understand longer or more formal translations.
- **Papago** to **talk** to people and have meaningful interactions with locals.

When [planning your trip to Japan](https://esim.holafly.com/travel-tips/how-to-plan-a-trip-to-japan/), do the following things before departure:

1. Install all three apps
2. Download offline Japanese packs for Google Translate and Papago (DeepL doesn’t have an offline mode).
3. Test each app to get familiar with how they work

I also recommend **testing Google Translate and Papago in airplane mode to understand their offline limitations.**

Only text translation works offline with Papago. With Google Translate, text and camera translation work without an internet connection (once the language pack is installed), but voice or conversation mode does not.

Therefore, **sorting a** [**travel eSIM**](https://esim.holafly.com/how-to/what-is-esim/) **before your departure** is crucial to using this three-way translation kit in a truly reliable way.

What’s more, every Holafly eSIM comes with [Always On](https://esim.holafly.com/always-on/), **1 GB of monthly backup data at no additional cost**. It activates automatically as long as the eSIM stays installed on your device, renews every month, and works across 150+ destinations. Install it before you fly, keep it on your phone, and let your translation apps do what they do best.

It depends… I’m talking about the kind of apps that can take a sentence- or even document-level input and give you back a translation in the blink of an eye. There are plenty of these free translation apps out there. Maybe you’ve heard of two of the most popular translation apps – Google Translate and DeepL – but which is better? What is the most accurate translation app? Is there one? As a professional Spanish to English translator and editor, it benefits me to keep up with the latest technology – adding gadgets to my translation toolbox when they facilitate my work and increase my productivity while discarding any that waste my time. So in the interest of full disclosure, I should mention that I don’t personally use these free translation apps or any AI-powered translation apps for my business. Nor do I offer machine-translation post editing as a service. I find that I get a better end result in about the same amount of time if I just do the translation from scratch, and that’s because I’ve been at this for years, so I can very often read a Spanish sentence and know exactly how I want to render it in English. My brain is my best translation app. I, for one, will never suggest you add [glue to pizza cheese](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jackkelly/2024/05/31/google-ai-glue-to-pizza-viral-blunders/) so it doesn’t slide off, as AI has. What’s more, I like flexing my brain and want to keep it healthy. A recent study used EEG tests to determine that over-reliance on ChatGPT can [decrease brain function](https://time.com/7295195/ai-chatgpt-google-learning-school/). ## How accurate are translation apps? Whether you’re using GoogleTranslate, DeepL, or an alternative, the best translation apps available today use something called neural machine translation or NMT. The systems are trained on huge amounts of text data to recognize patterns and relationships in language. They can then use that information to predict the most likely translation. But NMT output can only be as accurate as its input. Ever heard the phrase “garbage in, garbage out”? If NMT has high quality data – and lots of it – it can get things right. If it doesn’t, then it may just take a good guess or even get things seriously wrong. Let’s look at a quick example. The phrase “¿Qué quiere tomar?” is something you’ll hear often in restaurants and bars in Spain and Latin America. It’s how a server would ask you what you’d like to drink. But “quiere” can mean either “you want” or “he/she/they want(s)” depending on the context. And the word “tomar” can also mean “take,” so one accurate translation of this phrase is: “What does he want to take?” But that obviously doesn’t fit the context. This exemplifies a key concept in linguistics that we professional translators deal with on a daily basis: different languages differ in what they can and must express. In English, you have to use a subject (you) in that sentence (what would _you_ like to drink?), but it’s not required in Spanish. That means you’ll need more context to determine the subject because the verb “quiere” functions equally here for both third person and second-person formal. We need the context of a person ordering at a bar to properly translate the phrase. That said, all four of the free translation apps I tested got this one right, with some variation of “What would you like to drink?” One even went as far as to colloquialize it to “What’ll you have?” Of course, this is a common phrase that has been translated many times, so it shouldn’t surprise us that the apps have the data needed to generate the right translation. But what happens when translation apps have fewer translations to pick from? That’s where my test comes in. ## Which of the best translation apps did I look at? Google Translate is the most popular translation app (according to… Google), so it had to make the list. I also wanted to look at some Google Translate alternatives, so I picked DeepL, Reverso Context, and Spanish Dictionary.com. They all exist as apps for both Android and iPhone. Here’s a quick logistical comparison: | | Google Translate | DeepL | Reverso Context | SpanishDictionary.com | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Number of languages available | 249 | 35 | 28 | 1 | | Offline use? | Yes | No | Yes | Yes | | Voice-to-text feature? | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes (with premium) | Why these four translation apps? Google is pretty ubiquitous and has, by far, the most languages available. I tend to use Google Translate while traveling and/or when I don’t speak the language I’m trying to translate from. I use DeepL and Reverso Context’s dictionaries in my work, but I’d never actually used the translation feature until I started thinking about all these free translation apps, which one is the best, and how accurate they might be. And I included SpanishDictionary.com because I was curious if an app that focused on only one language would do a better job with it. ![](https://www.atanet.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/culture-300x169.jpg) ## Some of the best translation apps take a literature test How did I test the AI translation apps? Poetry. Not because I want the machine to fail, but because poetry is generally considered hard to translate; it’s so intensely personal and, well, human. It also uses language in a very non-literal way and leaves lots of room for interpretation. I chose “Ama tu ritmo” by Rubén Darío, a Nicaraguan poet, because it’s in the public domain, which means I can provide a translation here without violating intellectual property rights. To create a baseline for the test, I took a stab at the translation myself so English-language readers can at least get the meaning. Disclaimer: while I am not a machine, I am also not a poet. | | | | --- | --- | | Ama tu ritmo y ritma tus acciones
bajo su ley, así como tus versos;
eres un universo de universos
y tu alma una fuente de canciones. | Love your rhythm and set yourself to the beat
according to its law and your poetry;
you are a universe of universes
your soul, a wellspring of songs. | | La celeste unidad que presupones
hará brotar en ti mundos diversos,
y al resonar tus números dispersos
pitagoriza en tus constelaciones. | The celestial unity that you assume
will see diverse worlds bloom in you,
and as your scattered songs resonate
pythagorize in your constellations. | | Escucha la retórica divina
del pájaro del aire y la nocturna
irradiación geométrica adivina; | Listen to the divine rhetoric
of the flying bird, and discern
the night’s geometric radiation; | | mata la indiferencia taciturna
y engarza perla y perla cristalina
en donde la verdad vuelca su urna. | kill taciturn indifference
and string together pearl and glass bead
where truth tips its urn. | Now, it’s the machines’ turn. I gave each translation app one stanza to translate. The results are unedited. | | | | | --- | --- | --- | | Google Translate | Ama tu ritmo y ritma tus acciones
bajo su ley, así como tus versos;
eres un universo de universos
y tu alma una fuente de canciones. | Mother your rhythm and rhythm your actions
I am under your law, as are your verses;
you are a universe of universes
and your soul a fountain of songs. | | DeepL | La celeste unidad que presupones
hará brotar en ti mundos diversos,
y al resonar tus números dispersos
pitagoriza en tus constelaciones. | The celestial unity that you presuppose
will make sprout in you diverse worlds,
and to the resonance of your dispersed numbers
pitagoriza in your constellations. | | Reverso Context | Escucha la retórica divina
del pájaro del aire y la nocturna
irradiación geométrica adivina; | Listen to the divine rhetoric
of the bird of the air and night
geometric radiation fortune-teller; | | SpanishDictionary.com | mata la indiferencia taciturna
y engarza perla y perla cristalina
en donde la verdad vuelca su urna. | it kills taciturn indifference
and crisses pearl and crystalline pearl
where the truth overturns its urn. | **Takeaways** Can you mostly understand each translation? Sure. But the emphasis is on mostly. Let’s take a closer look at a few places where a human touch makes a difference. 1. **Google**: formal and informal address confusion. Google Translate incorrectly translated the line “bajo su ley, así como tus versos” – using third person rather than second-person formal. Google missed the broader context that a human translator would see; the very same line includes an informal “you,” which is a clue that the other possessive is third person. In Spanish, you don’t generally switch between the two when addressing one person. 2. **DeepL**: thwarted by made-up words. Poor DeepL was given a challenge with “pitagorizar” which is not actually a verb in Spanish, but it is being used like one. Rather than making up a similar word in English – for example, I opted for “pythagorize” – DeepL just left it in Spanish. I will give Google Translate credit on this one; it came up with the same solution I did here. Reverso Context went for “Pythagorean,” which doesn’t make grammatical sense. SpanishDictionary.com said “piitize,” so no comment there. 3. **Reverso Context**: It’s a noun; it’s a verb; it’s… “Adivina” is being used as a verb here in the third stanza. The syntax is admittedly a bit odd, but that’s poetry for you. Reverso Context assumes it’s a noun and translates it as “fortune-teller.” 4. **SpanishDictionary.com**: It’s definitely a verb, but what kind of verb? Finally, SpanishDictionary.com did recognize that “mata” (“kill”) is a verb, but it got the mode wrong because it didn’t recognize the imperative or command form. This, again, could be solved with context. The rest of the poem is written in the imperative. As such, I checked whether inputting the entire poem would yield a better result and… it actually did! On this, humans and machines agree: more context equals better results. That said, there was still quite a bit of room for improvement – and the apps even generated several typos (“sprout” became “sproup”). ![](https://www.atanet.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/network-300x169.jpg) ## The best translation app? Ultimately, I can’t say which is the best app for translating languages. They all did some things right and some things very wrong. Regardless, giving these four translation apps some poetic license has reminded me why my clients choose me over the machines. They pay me to use my brain and experience to deliver translations that a human would want to read. They know I’m sourcing terminology from the right contextual dictionaries; searching language forums and collaborating with colleagues when faced with subtle linguistic nuances or complex sentence structures; and proofreading my own work several times. That’s how I know I’m being more thorough than even the best translation app. I’m looking at the full context; considering the intended message and audience, the register, the imagery that might be used with the text; and so much more. All of this informs my choices and how I translate. From subtitles to marketing copy, it’s not just about what’s being said; it’s about how it’s being said and how the target audience will engage with it. So when asking yourself, “Are translation apps accurate?” the answer is, as always, “it depends on the context.” Translation apps are useful if you just need to get by in a foreign language – when you’re traveling and need to interact with the locals or need to get the gist of a document in a language other than your own. But often, style, tone, and flow are just as important as accuracy. Many professional translators use apps and other technology as tools before adding their own human touch. But I, for one, am convinced that the machines won’t be replacing me anytime soon.
